name: Gossamer-Throne
geological_features: Layered cloud systems spanning 2000 kilometers vertically
Possible solid core of exotic ice phases
specific_features: Gossamer-thin high-altitude cloud layer visible above the main atmosphere
Atmospheric microbial life floating in the temperate cloud bands
description: Gossamer-Throne is a gas giant distinguished by an extremely thin, high-altitude cloud layer that extends thousands of kilometers above the main atmospheric bands. This gossamer layer, composed of ice crystals so sparse they are nearly invisible from within, catches starlight and creates a faint luminous halo around the planet that is visible from great distances. The main atmosphere below is a complex stack of cloud bands in muted golds, browns, and cream, rotating at different speeds and generating shear zones where storms form and dissolve in cycles measured in weeks.

The most significant discovery about Gossamer-Throne was the detection of microbial life floating in the temperate cloud bands approximately five hundred kilometers below the cloud tops. These organisms are gas-bag floaters, tiny spheres of biological membrane filled with hydrogen that maintain neutral buoyancy in the atmosphere. They photosynthesize using the dim light that filters down from above and reproduce by budding, releasing daughter organisms that drift on atmospheric currents. Their total biomass is estimated in the billions of tonnes, a living layer within the atmosphere of a world with no solid surface.

The atmospheric microorganisms represent the only confirmed case of life evolving in a gas giant atmosphere, a possibility long theorized but never before observed. Their biochemistry is based on familiar carbon-hydrogen chemistry but adapted to the extreme conditions of their environment—high pressure, low light, and a hydrogen-helium medium rather than the oxygen-nitrogen atmospheres where most known life operates. They appear to have no predators and no competitors, drifting in their temperate layer in vast, slow-moving clouds of living gas bubbles.

Studying the floater organisms requires operating within the gas giant's atmosphere, a technically demanding proposition that has been achieved through the deployment of instrumented aerostats. These research platforms drift alongside the organism clouds, collecting samples and monitoring their life cycles over periods of months. The data has already challenged fundamental assumptions about the conditions required for life to emerge and persist. Gossamer-Throne has become the most important site in astrobiology, proof that life can take root in environments previously considered utterly impossible, floating like gossamer in the atmosphere of a world that is itself nothing but atmosphere.
